# Mercury and amalgamation of gold and silver (`mercury_amalgam`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/materials.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Metallurgy & materials (`materials`)
- Deps: helped by distillation, salt_production
- Core idea: Red cinnabar roasted at about 600 °C gives mercury vapour, which condenses to the liquid metal on a cool surface. Mercury wets and dissolves gold and silver. Crushed gold ore or river sand is worked over mercury, the pasty amalgam is squeezed through leather and then heated in a closed retort, so the mercury distils off to be used again and the gold stays. For low-grade silver ore (patio process), the ground ore is spread wet in a yard and mixed with salt, roasted copper pyrites and mercury, trodden for weeks, washed, and the amalgam retorted. Gold amalgam brushed on to metal and heated gives fire gilding.
- Pitfalls:
  - Mercury vapour has no smell and destroys nerves and kidneys; heating amalgam in the open poisons the worker and the household. Always distil in a closed retort outdoors.
  - It is not safe at room temperature either; spilt mercury in a warm room poisons slowly.
  - Mercury was long used as a medicine; it causes loosened teeth, tremor and madness rather than cure.
  - Expecting it to work on all ores; sulphide silver ores need salt and a copper salt, and some gold is too fine or coated to amalgamate.
  - Losing the mercury; it is dear, and about as much is lost as silver is won.
- History: china: c. 2nd millennium BC cinnabar as pigment; 210 BC rivers of mercury reported in the tomb of Qin Shi Huang; amalgam gilding by the Warring States period; greece: c. 300 BC – Theophrastus describes obtaining quicksilver from cinnabar; rome: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD – Vitruvius and Pliny describe recovering gold with mercury and fire gilding; mines at Almadén; islamic: 10th–12th c. – amalgamation of gold ores described (al-Hamdani, al-Biruni); Almadén worked under the caliphate; americas: cinnabar used as pigment in the pre-Columbian Andes and Mesoamerica; 1554 Bartolomé de Medina's patio process at Pachuca; 1570s adopted at Potosí with mercury from Huancavelica; europe: medieval fire gilding (Theophilus); 1540 Biringuccio describes amalgamating silver ore; 1887 the cyanide process begins to replace mercury
- Read:
  - Vitruvius, De architectura VII.8
  - Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540)
  - Nicholas A. Robins, Mercury, Mining, and Empire: The Human and Ecological Cost of Colonial Silver Mining in the Andes (2011)
